summary:
Tanzania's Penal Code criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with imprisonment of up to life available as a maximum penalty. Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 inserted section 138A, under which "gross indecency" between men is an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 shillings for the general case; the offence as charged can reach life. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also prohibited, so exposure to criminal law does not depend on the gender of a partner.

The semi-autonomous island jurisdiction of Zanzibar operates its own criminal statute, the Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives, alongside the Zanzibar Penal Code of 1934 as amended in 2004. Zanzibar's code outlaws sex between women with a penalty of up to five years' imprisonment or a fine of 500,000 shillings, and the 2004 Act defines "gross indecency" broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, with absolute age thresholds below 12 and distinct provisions for under-18s and married persons. A visitor therefore moves between two overlapping criminal-law regimes depending on location, and the wording of the offence differs between them.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania. A partner cannot be sponsored for immigration, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin on the basis of relationship status, and adoption requires a married couple, which excludes joint adoption by a same-sex pair. These consequences fall on visitors through border and estate procedure as much as through criminal law.

Enforcement has taken organisational as well as individual forms. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the grounds that they were promoting homosexuality, an action that disrupted treatment services. In 2018 the Regional Commissioner of Dar es Salaam, Paul Makonda, announced a seventeen-member committee of police, lawyers and doctors tasked with identifying and punishing homosexual people, and searched the internet for videos of purportedly LGBTQ individuals; the same year a "witch hunt" against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam in which gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and were tortured. The Foreign Ministry subsequently stated that the crackdown lacked government support, and Denmark withheld 65 million krone, about 9.8 million US dollars, in aid.

Ill-treatment in custody is documented. A 2013 report by Human Rights Watch and the Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition recorded torture of LGBT people by police, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said officers raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. The United States State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania likewise details abuse in police custody, lists discrimination based on sexual orientation among the country's significant problems, and characterises the human rights record as poor.

Violence against trans people continues into 2024. In June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as "horrendous" the attack on Mauzinde, a Tanzanian transgender activist from Rahaleo, who was abducted by twelve men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut off. The UN called for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people and flagged possible violations of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights article 20 and of the equality guarantees in article 13 of Tanzania's Constitution.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report, "We Are Facing Extinction," documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people at national level, and records that proposed legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests. The report situates those developments within a documented climate of discrimination that limits how far rights can be enjoyed in practice.

The information environment is constrained. OONI's 2024 report, "Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship," records state-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites, social networks and rights organisations based on measurement data. Government respect for freedom of speech and of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals.

Non-discrimination obligations exist in health policy on paper. The 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, colour or sexual preference; the Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care on grounds of sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. Set against that, Tanzania has a high HIV prevalence, reported at about one million people infected, and health services for sexual minorities have previously been disrupted by state action.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of official rhetoric matters for expectations on the ground. Openly stated hostility came from named officials including John Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, and was met by public counter-statements from activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule. Activists who have taken that position have done so in a climate where reprisals are a stated concern, so visibility carries risk.

Broadcast and online content rules have shifted more than once. The 2018 broadcast content regulations barred inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference, and online content regulations issued the same year banned equivalent hate speech, but those online regulations were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation, leaving self-regulation rather than statute carrying that prohibition online.

Interview research with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists, published in September 2020, records substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia given as the driving urgency behind rights advocacy. The picture aligns with the country profiles maintained by human rights litigation organisations, although the Human Dignity Trust country profile could not be retrieved at research time.

As a comparison point, the 2013 United States State Department report named security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including female genital mutilation and cutting, and lack of access to justice as the three most widespread problems in Tanzania, alongside discrimination based on sexual orientation and societal violence against persons with albinism. Security-force conduct is therefore a general rather than a niche risk.
localsOnly:
Legal recognition is unavailable to Tanzanian residents as well as visitors. Same-sex couples cannot marry or register a partnership, cannot be treated as next of kin for medical or burial decisions, and cannot adopt jointly, since adoption is conditioned on marriage. Where a resident's partner dies, relationship status confers no inheritance route.

Media professionals work under the Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals, which prohibits hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation, while the 2018 broadcast content regulations bar incitement to hatred on grounds of sexual preference.

Residents have grounds to claim non-discriminatory treatment in clinical settings: the Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care on grounds of sexual orientation, the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory practice, and the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to counselling any woman, man, couple or young person regardless of age and to services regardless of sexual preference. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond that age-inclusive counselling language is stated in the sources.

Social venues are limited. There are no gay bars in Tanzania, though some places exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. Community organising has nonetheless produced sustained public advocacy by named activists and by organisations such as Rahaleo.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania returned HTTP 403 at research time, so the criminalisation and life-imprisonment figures attributed to it are carried from the underlying profile and its text could not be read directly in this pass. This is unresolved rather than confirmed.

Whether section 138A's maximum of life imprisonment has been imposed in a reported case in recent years is not sourced here; the inventory supplies statutory maximums and documented enforcement episodes, not a sentence survey. Whether Zanzibar's authorities apply the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 alongside the Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, and how the two are charged in practice, is likewise not stated in the sources.

The inventory does not establish current visa, entry-screening or document-marker rules for travellers, including whether passport gender markers are inspected or altered at the border. Nor does it establish the present status of the deferred legislation on same-sex relations beyond its deferral after protests. No source in this inventory reports a court judgment on the constitutionality of the criminal provisions; the UN's reference to article 13 of the Constitution and ICCPR article 20 was made in relation to a specific attack, not as a ruling.
